articles.summary: CHANDIGARH: Punjabi social media influencer Manjeet Kaur died at PGIMER nearly two months after she was allegedly abducted from Chandigarh, taken to a.
articles.body: CHANDIGARH: Punjabi social media influencer Manjeet Kaur died at PGIMER nearly two months after she was allegedly abducted from Chandigarh, taken to a forested area near Morinda, tied to a tree and set on fire.Kaur died on August 26 while undergoing treatment for severe burn injuries.Chandigarh Police have now registered a case of abduction and murder after her mother, Kanta Devi, approached the police.The case has also raised questions over the alleged failure of Punjab Police to record Kaur’s statement when she was reportedly conscious and had expressed her intention to give one.Also check: Who was Manjeet Kaur? Inside the life of Punjabi influencerAlleged abduction and attackAccording to Kanta Devi’s complaint, two acquaintances of her daughter, Shubhi and Pinda, called Kaur to Sector 34 in Chandigarh on the intervening night of July 3 and 4.They allegedly assaulted her, forced her into a vehicle and took her to a forested area near Morinda in Punjab.Police said the two allegedly tied Kaur to a tree and set her on fire before fleeing the spot.Another acquaintance later reached the area and reportedly extinguished the flames using a blanket.Kaur was taken to a hospital in Morinda and later treated at Max Hospital in Mohali. She was subsequently shifted to PGIMER in Chandigarh, where she remained under treatment until her death.Questions over police responseThe case has brought the response of Kharar Sadar police under scrutiny.Sources said Kaur regained consciousness during her treatment at PGIMER and wanted to have her statement recorded.Kaur, or one of her acquaintances, reportedly contacted police from the hospital after she regained consciousness.The PGIMER police post also informed Kharar Sadar police that Kaur was conscious and in a condition to give her statement.The information was reportedly passed on to the investigating officer, but he allegedly did not reach the hospital.A daily diary report (DDR) regarding the communication was also recorded at the PGI police post, sources said.Despite this, no case was registered during the nearly two months Kaur remained under treatment.FIR registered after her deathKaur died at PGIMER on August 26.Following her death, the PGI police post again sent a communication to Kharar Sadar police.The investigating officer subsequently reached the hospital.Kaur’s mother was later taken to the Sector 34 police station in Chandigarh, where her statement was recorded and an FIR was registered on Wednesday night.Her postmortem was conducted at PGIMER on Thursday, after which her body was handed over to the family.Chandigarh Police begin investigationChandigarh Police are now investigating the circumstances surrounding the alleged abduction and attack.Investigators are examining why Kaur had gone to Sector 34, the vehicle allegedly used to abduct her and the motive behind the attack.Police are also examining CCTV footage from Sector 34 and adjoining areas.Toll-plaza camera footage is likely to be checked to trace the vehicle allegedly used to transport Kaur from Chandigarh to Morinda.Investigators will also examine whether the two hospitals where Kaur was treated before being shifted to PGIMER informed police about the medico-legal case (MLC).Police to verify earlier complaintsKaur reportedly lived in Sunny Enclave, while her mother and brother reside in Sector 19, Panchkula.Chandigarh Police will also verify articles.title: Fears Digbeth faces cultural wipeout if rail expansion goes ahead
articles.summary: Music venue owners say the area is the heart of nightlife in Birmingham which needs saving.
articles.body:
For fans of music and arts in Birmingham, Digbeth is area which inspires a lot of positive feelings as the graffiti-covered old industrial heartland that is home to the city's main music, nightclub and art scene.

But Digbeth is facing an uncertain future.

Nightclubs and community venues in the area are warning that a major railway project could lead to a "complete cultural wipe out" of the bohemian district..

Dozens of independent music venues and community spaces could be demolished if a huge redevelopment project, the £1.75bn Midlands Rail Hub between Birmingham Moor Street and Bordesley stations, goes ahead.

"Pretty much every venue and cultural space" in Digbeth would close under the current plans, according to Dan Ickowitz-Seidler, co-owner of nightclub XOYO Birmingham.

Those behind the project, the Midlands Rail Hub Alliance, have tried to reassure Digbeth's many fans, saying they see how the plans could affect businesses and promise a further consultation as the project develops.

The plans were a "real shock", Ickowitz-Seidler said, adding they were "blindsided" after finding out about the scheme from a post on X.

There appeared to be little consideration for properties based along Lower Trinity Street, he said, which houses popular venues such as Luna Springs, Mama Roux's and Club Colette.

"We all were completely shocked of just how this had all come out of the blue," he said.

"There was talk about redeveloping Digbeth for quite a long time, but that was different plans, and that was still incorporating the nightlife and all the culture that happens there.

"This very much kind of blindsided us and came out the blue."

That would see sections of the existing Bordesley Viaduct, which runs through Digbeth and into Moor Street, widened, with two new railway platforms built.

These changes would cut congestion and transfer a number of services to Moor Street from New Street, Network Rail said, reducing congestion at that station.

But some firms said their premises would be demolished if the scheme goes ahead and they would have to close by 2030.

The railway plans were good for the city, Ickowitz-Seidler added, but said there should be a compromise to save the venues so "they don't have to be destroyed".

"We're not saying that the work shouldn't happen," he explained.

"But I'm hoping that an alternative can be found that the works can happen in some way and the venues can also be saved."

He warned that without changes to the plans: "It's highly likely that all these venues will become just parts of history and no longer here".

"Digbeth has grown organically over many years to become this cultural hub." he added.

"I think it's the heart of nightlife and the heart of kind of musical, music culture in Birmingham."

Digbeth has played host to a number of artists over the years, including Walsall-born Jorja Smith and Brit Award-winning artist Little Simz, as well as Patrick Topping, Pawsa and DJ Jamie Jones.

In a joint statement on Instagram, clubs Mama Roux's and Club Colette, which is also the birthplace of popular street food pioneers Digbeth Dining Club , said the street was a "launchpad for UK culture" and was facing "total cultural erasure".

"We don't just host nights out. we actively invest directly in local musicians, performers and grassroots talent every single week," the venues said.

Digbeth was home to the "most concentrated area of independent music venues," Benjy Hill, Mama's operations manager, said.

The area was a "mix of everything", he added, with dance and electronic music, live music acts, cabaret and jazz nights.

It was a misconception that Digbeth was "just a place full of nightclubs", Hill said, adding the creative spaces were "super important", against competition like London and Manchester.

Referring to previous HS2 works, for the high speed line, he said major infrastructure projects had "stripped the heart out" of the area, arguing that venues could struggle to operate during any disruption, even if their buildings were not demolished.

"You're not going to be able to operate with all that work going on around you," he explained.

"If the area becomes really disjointed during the works, it's not going to be a nightlife area because for a nightlife area to thrive, you need everything kind of working together."

Venue owners were generally in favour of a railway extension if it brought more people to the area, Hill stressed, but affected venues would need to be relocated together.

"We need to be rehoused collectively or something like that," he said.

"If we found a new home but XOYO were two miles away further, it just wouldn't work."

Digbeth is also home to the The Night Owl music venue and The Warehouse, used by Birmingham Friends of the Earth.

Shannon Davies, from The Night Owl, previously described how the venue had played an important role in the city's cultural scene and had hosted weddings.

"Whether we are flattened, used as a construction site, or impossible to get to, we won't survive it," she said.

Better Streets for Birmingham, whose monthly meeting takes place at The Warehouse on Allison Street, said the Midlands Rail Hub plan was of "vital importance to the future of rail travel in the city and wider region".

"New Street Station is full. The proposals currently being consulted on will create rail capacity," they said in a statement.

But a spokesperson emphasised that the plans could be amended.

"We would also stress that we think the plans can be better shaped to avoid loss of buildings," they said.

"So [we] encourage businesses and organisations to engage with the consultation on the basis that plans can still be shaped towards a better mutual outcome."

A consultation on the proposed upgrades came to an end on Friday.

articles.title: 'Suddhikaran another name for untouchability': Rahul Gandhi accuses BJP, RSS of discrimination against Kharge
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Saturday attacked the Bharatiya Janata Party and Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh over a recent '.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Saturday attacked the Bharatiya Janata Party and Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh over a recent 'suddhikaran' or 'purification' ritual held at a venue in Uttarakhand where Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge had addressed a rally.Calling the practice "another name for untouchability", Rahul alleged that such an act was a crime under the Constitution.Addressing a presser at Congress headquarters in Delhi, the Rae Bareli MP said the country was witnessing a political contest between the ideology of the Constitution and that of the BJP and RSS."Our CLP leader in Rajasthan visits a temple, and BJP leaders perform a 'purification' ritual. Congress President Kharge ji, who has dedicated his entire life to the country and the Constitution, goes to the Ramlila Ground in Haldwani to deliver a speech, and a purification ritual is performed there. Who does this? It is the people from the BJP and RSS," Rahul said."Only BJP and RSS members do this, and it is a crime. Under India's Constitution, this is a crime, a criminal activity. 'Purification' is actually just another name for untouchability. Untouchability was outlawed, yet BJP members practice it openly," he added.Former Congress president said the ritual suggested that Dalits were "unclean" and should not be touched."When they perform this purification, they are effectively saying that Dalits should not be touched, that Dalits are unclean, and this constitutes a crime under the Indian Constitution," he said.Rahul also said the larger political contest in the country was between two opposing ideologies."A fight is under way in the country between two ideologies. On one side is the Constitution of India, the Constitution of Ambedkar, Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Sardar Patel. On the other is the ideology of the BJP and RSS. The politics currently playing out in India is between these two ideologies," Rahul said.He also spoke about alleged caste-based discrimination and said Dalits continue to face discrimination despite constitutional safeguards."For thousands of years, Dalits in this country have been subjected to atrocities and violence. While the Constitution made this illegal, even today, Dalit children in schools are made to clean toilets and sweep and mop floors," he said."Just think about the impact this has on the minds of the future generation: children see some of their peers sweeping, while those doing the sweeping see others who do not have to do so. This is the reality of India," he added.Congress leader further alleged that caste discrimination was also visible in access to common resources such as water."Dalits are not allowed to drink water from the village well; they have had to dig their own private wells because they were barred from using the common village well," Rahul claimed.He also alleged that caste discrimination could be seen at tea stalls."At tea stalls, you see two types of cups in use: a reusable glass cup that can be washed, and a paper or plastic cup that is discarded after use. The plastic or paper cups are for Dalits, while the glass ones are for others," he alleged."This is the reality of India. This is the reality of Uttar Pradesh, the reality of North India, and you can see this in cities and villages," Rahul added.The Haldwani controversy relates to a Congress rally held at Ramlila Maidan on August 8, ahead of the 2027 Uttarakhand assembly elections. Members of a right-wing group later performed a purification ritual at the venue, drawing criticism from Congress leaders.Kharge also raised the issue in the Rajya Sabha, linking the incident to his identity as a Dalit leader and alleging that it was an attempt to portray him as "untouchable".Kharge said he did not mention any community or religion during his speech at the venue."But after my speech, people associated with the BJP carried out a 'purification' ritual of that stage. You may have read about this in the newspapers. Is this the way things should happen in a democracy? How are you protecting the Constitution?" Kharge had said.He later took to X and said he did not want the incident to be politicised, while calling for strict legal action and demanding that a case be filed under the Untouchability Act against those who conducted the ritual.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A wooden relic that survived the sack of Jerusalem's First Temple was unearthed by archaeologists, now they are finding shocking answers
articles.summary: Middle East News: In the current world, it is highly unlikely to come across intact wood that is thousands of years old and yet untouched. During an archaeological exca.
articles.body: In the current world, it is highly unlikely to come across intact wood that is thousands of years old and yet untouched. During an archaeological excavation in the area known as the Givati Parking Lot in the City of David, a team of researchers recently uncovered charred remains dating to the Iron Age, from the time of the destruction of Jerusalem's First Temple in 586 B.C. as per a report by AS. Alongside these fragments, researchers also found conifer wood containing numerous well-preserved growth rings.A preserved relicThe thick beams discovered were made of sycamore wood and as per experts, once formed part of the roof of an interior courtyard. Efrat Bocher, an excavation director, said that the beams "appear to have served as the roof of an inner courtyard." "During the destruction, they collapsed onto the floor," Bocher said in a statement.They date back to roughly 2,600 years, likely the remnants of the destruction of Solomon's Temple. The discovery was announced by the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA) in July. IAA officials said the wood was found "within a building that collapsed by the intense fire at the time of the First Temple's destruction."Their statement added, "What likely preserved the beams for approximately 2,600 years was plaster that melted from the building's walls, sealing the burnt wood beneath it."The big question is how they managed to survive for so long. The answer lies in the very fire that destroyed the building. When the flames consumed the structure, the timbers collapsed to the ground and were immediately covered by plaster from the walls, which the intense heat had altered. This layer of material acted as a nearly perfect protective seal, preventing the remains from disintegrating over the centuries.Researcher Johanna Regev explained that combining the analysis of these rings with modern radiocarbon testing makes it possible to determine dates with much greater precision. Until now, experts often had to work with margins of error spanning hundreds of years when dating objects this ancient. With this material, however, the time frame can be narrowed to just a decade.Preserved among the ruinsSolomon's Temple, also called the First Temple, was destroyed by Babylonian King Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 B.C., after his army captured Jerusalem following a lengthy siege. It was originally built by King Solomon in the 10th century B.C. as the permanent house for the Ark of the Covenant, according to Scripture. The destruction of Solomon's Temple ushered in the Second Temple period, the era of Judaism in which Jesus lived and practised.Experts leading the project believe that the people who returned to the city decades after the sack made a conscious decision not to clear the area, leaving the burned remains exactly where they lay. The purpose of this act may have been to keep the memory of the disaster alive, with new streets later built directly over the ashes."Preserving memory is a human need, seeking to preserve what once existed," excavation director Yiftah Shalev said in a statement. "Here we see it in its clearest form: a deliberate choice to leave ruins in place as a testament to the destruction and build the new layer over them."This historic discovery also coincides on the calendar with the traditional dates commemorating the fall of the ancient city at the hands of the Babylonians. The event is still remembered in the region each year through Tisha B’Av, which involves various days of mourning and fasting.In a statement, Bocher called the discovery "deeply moving." It "makes you feel that you are witnessing the very moment of destruction, the moment when it all happened," she said.Jerusalem, known as the Eternal City, is the setting of countless notable archaeological discoveries per year. Last year, archaeologists in Jerusalem uncovered the longest and best-preserved section of the city's Hasmonean-era wall. And earlier this year, excavators uncovered a "mysterious and impressive" ancient tunnel near Jerusalem's biblical-era Kingdom of Judah.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Do you feel you are a lord?’ Bombay HC slams FDA, clears reopening of 5 eateries
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court on slammed the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA), warning of contempt action against officials after the.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court on slammed the Maharashtra Food and Drug Administration (FDA), warning of contempt action against officials after the department refused to lift the suspension of food licences of five restaurants at the Mumbai Cricket Association (MCA) premises despite a fresh inspection finding them 88% compliant with food safety rules.“Tired of scolding the department and officers,” the division bench of Acting Chief Justice Ravindra Ghuge and Justice Gautam Ankhad said the FDA had taken a “pedantic instead of pragmatic view” despite the court’s earlier direction to reconsider the matter. The court ultimately vacated the suspension orders, allowing the five eateries at the MCA premises in Bandra-Kurla Complex (BKC) to reopen.The MCA had challenged the FDA’s decision to suspend the restaurants’ licences over alleged hygiene violations and issues relating to third-party operations. A fresh inspection conducted on Thursday found the eateries to be 88% compliant with food safety requirements.However, the FDA had initially continued with the suspension, citing the fact that the restaurants were being operated by M/s Shirke Infrastructure, while the licences were registered in the MCA’s name.On Saturday, the FDA told the court that it would issue a fresh notice to the MCA, give it an opportunity to be heard on its contractual arrangement with Shirke Infrastructure and then pass a reasoned order.Accepting the undertaking, the court said the restaurants could reopen since the latest inspection had found them compliant. “There is no provision in the law that prohibits the same,” the bench observed.The court recalled that it had, during the previous hearing, specifically directed FDA officials to apply their minds and take a pragmatic approach to the licence issue.“However, despite clearly saying this, the FDA has disobeyed our order and taken a pedantic view instead of a pragmatic view. We are tired of scolding the department and officers all the time. It is now time to pass stinging orders. We will issue contempt action against the concerned officers. Let them convince us or go to jail," the court said.The bench also questioned why the FDA acted with “undue haste” without fully analysing the legal position.“How many times should we try to convince and balance equities so that the department does not feel discouraged? Why do we say don't kill a mosquito with a sword? Do you feel you are a lord and you can do anything?” HC questioned.The dispute began after the FDA suspended the five licences last week. At Tuesday’s hearing, the HC had praised FDA commissioner Tukaram Mundhe’s drive against hygiene lapses but asked the department to “be consistent” and “do it consistently and not in an ad hoc manner”.The court had ordered a fresh inspection while declining to stay the suspensions, though it allowed MCA to serve tea and coffee through vending machines as a temporary arrangement during ongoing tournaments.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The AAP on Saturday challenged the BJP to take action against three of the party’s Lok Sabha MPs from Delhi for attending the condolence meeting of former Congress leader Sajjan Kumar, a convict in the 1984 anti-Sikh riots.Kumar, 80, died in Delhi on August 20 while serving life imprisonment in a case related to the anti-Sikh riots.According to BJP leader HS Phoolka, an advocate who represented victims of the 1984 violence and their families, party MPs Kamaljeet Sehrawat, Ramvir Singh Bidhuri, and Yogender Chandolia visited Kumar's residence to offer condolences following his death.AAP Delhi chief Saurabh Bharadwaj claimed that the BJP was “sympathetic” towards Kumar, alleging that the saffron party had “helped” the Congress in targeting Sikh families during the 1984 riots."Some people do say that during the anti-Sikh riots in Delhi, local BJP/RSS leaders helped congress in targeting innocent Sikh families on the streets of Delhi. Is this the reason why top BJP leaders of Delhi are so sympathetic to Sajjan Kumar?" Bharadwaj posted on X."Will @NitinNabin suspend these MPs of BJP who have backstabbed Sikhs?" he added, tagging the BJP national president.Bhardwaj also questioned the “silence” of Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) leaders on the issue. Sympathy should be reserved for victims and their families—many of whom live the horror of those days even till now,” Phoolka wrote.Phoolka also called for a “boycott” of the three MPs.The anti-Sikh riots broke out following the October 31, 1984, assassination of then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by her Sikh bodyguards. articles.title: Swaran Jayanti Ashray Yojana: Himachal scheme offers Rs 1.5 lakh assistance for house construction
articles.summary: News News: Having a house of one’s own can be difficult for families with limited financial resources, particularly when the cost of construction continues to ma.
articles.body: Having a house of one’s own can be difficult for families with limited financial resources, particularly when the cost of construction continues to make it harder to turn available land into a permanent home. For eligible residents of Himachal Pradesh, the state government has a scheme aimed at providing financial support for constructing a new house.The Swaran Jayanti Ashray Yojana, launched by the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of Himachal Pradesh, provides financial assistance to eligible beneficiaries belonging to Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST) and Other Backward Classes (OBC), who do not have their own house.Under the scheme, eligible beneficiaries can receive financial assistance of Rs 1,50,000 for the construction of a new house.Who is eligible for the scheme?The applicant must fulfil the following conditions:• The applicant should be a permanent resident of Himachal Pradesh.• The applicant should belong to the SC, ST or OBC category.• The applicant's annual income should not exceed Rs 50,000.• The applicant should not own a house.• The land intended for construction should be in the applicant's name in the revenue records.Documents requiredApplicants need to submit documents including a Himachali Certificate issued by the executive magistrate, a caste certificate and an annual income certificate.Other required documents include Tatima and Jamabandi of the land on which the house is proposed to be constructed, the Gram Sabha proposal, spot report, No Objection Certificate (NOC), proposal and a photograph of the house verified by the Pradhan.How to apply?The application process for the scheme is offline. Interested applicants can download the prescribed application form from the official website and fill in all the mandatory details. Copies of the required documents should also be attached, with self-attestation wherever required.The completed and signed application form, along with the supporting documents, should then be submitted to the concerned district welfare officer or tehsil welfare officer.Applicants should request a receipt or acknowledgement at the time of submission. The receipt should contain details such as the date and time of submission and a unique identification number, if applicable.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Meet Wesley Goodridge, the Grade 7 Canadian student who built a device to test milk freshness before throwing it away; he won a $10,000 scholarship
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Wesley Goodridge, a Grade 7 student at Aberfoyle Public School in Morriston, Ontario, won gold in the junior category at the 2026 Canada-Wide Science .
articles.body: Wesley Goodridge, a Grade 7 student at Aberfoyle Public School in Morriston, Ontario, won gold in the junior category at the 2026 Canada-Wide Science Fair for a project tackling an everyday source of food waste: milk that gets thrown away before consumers know whether it has actually spoiled. His project, Test Before You Toss, explores whether a scientific measurement could give people a more reliable way to assess milk freshness than simply relying on a best-before date or their own senses. Goodridge also received the Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Challenge Award and a $10,000 university scholarship. His project grew out of an interest in food waste that began during a trip to Rome with his father, University of Guelph food professor Lawrence Goodridge. At the national science fair in Edmonton, held from May 23 to 30, 2026, the young researcher presented his approach alongside students from across Canada.How a trip to Rome sparked Wesley Goodridge's science-fair ideaAccording to the Wellington Advertiser, Goodridge's interest in food waste began during a trip to Rome with his father, Lawrence Goodridge, who was working with the United Nations' Food and Agriculture Organisation. A large display about food waste in a cafeteria caught the student's attention and led him to think about how much food gets discarded simply because people cannot easily determine whether it is still usable. Goodridge has said that science has always been part of his life because of his father, a food professor and Canada Research Chair in food-borne pathogen dynamics at the University of Guelph. His project turned that interest into an experiment focused on one of the most common foods found in household refrigerators.Why Goodridge focused on ATP to investigate milk freshnessInstead of trying to identify individual bacteria, Goodridge's project uses adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, as an indicator of biological activity. ATP is present in living cells, including microorganisms, making it possible to use ATP measurements as an indicator of microbial activity in a sample. For Test Before You Toss, Goodridge investigated whether measuring ATP could provide useful information about the freshness of milk. The approach is designed around giving consumers additional information when deciding whether milk should still be used, rather than relying only on the date printed on the container or traditional sensory checks. The project earned Goodridge the Agriculture, Fisheries and Food Challenge Award at the Canada-Wide Science Fair, recognising its focus on a practical food-related problem.How Test Before You Toss could help reduce food wasteThe basic idea behind Goodridge's project is to give consumers another tool for deciding what to do with milk that may be approaching the end of its usable life. A best-before date does not automatically mean that a food has become unsafe, but uncertainty about freshness can lead people to throw products away rather than risk consuming them. A test capable of providing additional information about a food's condition could therefore help reduce unnecessary waste. Goodridge's project combines that food-waste problem with a scientific measurement, turning a question that normally comes down to a smell test or a printed date into something that can instead be investigated experimentally.What Goodridge has already tested and where the project could go nextGoodridge's experiments have already included milk with three different fat percentages, allowing him to examine how the composition of the milk affects the results. That work forms part of the project's current research rather than being a future experiment he has yet to undertake. The project could eventually be developed into a more accessible system for consumers. Goodridge has also explored the possibility of using a photo-based app, which could make the technology easier for people to use outside a laboratory setting. His work at the national science fair was supported by the Canadian Black Scientists Network following his success at regional science fairs. He now hopes to continue developing the project and investigate whether the approach can eventually be applied more broadly. For a Grade 7 student, Goodridge's project starts with a remarkably ordinary question: before throwing food away, can science provide a better answer about whether it is still good?Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1954, aviation pioneer Glenn L. Martin donated over 2,500 acres of his Chesapeake Bay hunting preserve; today the refuge spans 4,548 acres and protects migratory birds
articles.summary: US News: A piece of Chesapeake Bay marshland that once formed part of an aviation pioneer's private hunting preserve has become an important refuge for wildlif.
articles.body: A piece of Chesapeake Bay marshland that once formed part of an aviation pioneer's private hunting preserve has become an important refuge for wildlife. What began as a donation of thousands of acres more than seven decades ago now protects tidal marshes, creeks, coves and wooded ridges used by migratory birds throughout the year. The landscape is part of a larger story of how privately held land can become a lasting habitat when it is placed under conservation management. Today, the refuge provides seasonal shelter for waterfowl, nesting grounds for numerous birds and habitat for mammals, reptiles and marine species, while also preserving a distinctive part of the Chesapeake Bay's natural landscape. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service records that Martin National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1954 after Glenn L. Martin donated 2,569 acres to the Service.From private preserve to refugeThe refuge occupies the northern half of Smith Island, about 11 miles west of Crisfield, Maryland, along with Watts Island farther south in the Chesapeake Bay. Its landscape is dominated by tidal marsh, with a network of creeks and coves, freshwater potholes and slightly elevated ridges supporting shrubs and trees. Offshore shallow waters also contain submerged aquatic vegetation, which provides an important food source for waterfowl. When Martin donated the property in 1954, the goal was no longer simply to preserve land for private recreation. The newly established refuge was intended to provide habitat for wildlife, particularly birds that depend on the Chesapeake Bay during migration and winter.The refuge's size has increased considerably since its creation. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Martin National Wildlife Refuge now spans 4,548 acres, following additional land purchases and donations over the years.A seasonal haven for birdsThe refuge's marshes and protected waters make it particularly valuable to migratory birds. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service describes the area as an important resting and wintering site for thousands of waterfowl. Winter visitors include black ducks, pintails, mergansers, long-tailed ducks, scoters, buffleheads, Canada geese and tundra swans. Historical records show that wintering waterfowl populations at the refuge could be substantial. The refuge has historically supported large numbers of wintering waterfowl, including ducks, Canada geese and tundra swans. These populations illustrate why protecting the marsh and surrounding shallow waters became an important part of refuge management.The habitat is not only important in winter. During spring and summer, marsh grasses, insects and underwater vegetation attract ducks including black ducks, mallards, gadwalls and green-winged teal for nesting. Gulls, terns, black skimmers, American oystercatchers and willets also use the marshes, mudflats and sandbars.Beyond waterfowlAlthough migratory waterfowl are central to the refuge's purpose, the protected landscape supports a much broader community of wildlife. Wooded ridges provide nesting locations for wading birds, while groups of herons, egrets and glossy ibis have established nesting colonies. Several species, including glossy ibis, little blue herons, tricoloured herons and several egret species, have been observed in rookeries on the refuge. Martin National Wildlife Refuge also supports the largest colony of brown pelicans in Maryland's portion of Chesapeake Bay.The marshes are home to mammals including red foxes, muskrats, mink, otters and voles. Northern diamondback terrapins and various nonvenomous water snakes also inhabit the area. Clapper rails, seaside sparrows and marsh wrens depend on the marsh habitat, while peregrine falcons have nested at the refuge since the installation of a nesting tower in 1984.A refuge shaped by the bayThe conservation value of Martin National Wildlife Refuge extends beyond birds and land animals. Its marshes and estuarine waters contribute to the Chesapeake Bay food web, supporting marine organisms such as crabs and oysters. The refuge is therefore part of a much larger ecological system in which wetlands, shallow waters, vegetation and wildlife are closely connected. The land also carries a long human history. Smith Island was explored and charted by Captain John Smith in 1608, while settlers later raised cattle on parts of the island. For more than three centuries, island communities have depended on Chesapeake Bay resources, particularly oysters and crabs. Evidence of old livestock corrals and low dikes built to hold back tides remains visible in parts of the landscape.What began with Martin's 2,569-acre donation has therefore become more than a preserved piece of land. Expanded to 4,548 acres, Martin National Wildlife Refuge now protects a changing mosaic of marshes, waterways and ridges that wildlife uses throughout the year. Its history demonstrates how a single land donation can eventually become part of a much larger conservation legacy, one that continues to provide habitat for thousands of migratory birds and other species along the Chesapeake Bay.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament
articles.summary: The imminent return of Parliament will put the new prime minister under real scrutiny, with MPs finally getting a chance to grill him.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham is set to come under the most intense scrutiny of his political life when Parliament returns on Tuesday.

Since coming to power six weeks ago, the new prime minister has largely been free to set his own agenda.

The timing of Labour's leadership contest meant he walked into Number 10 after the House of Commons began its summer break, denying MPs the chance to question him and creating what some have seen as a honeymoon period.

Burnham has embarked on what Downing Street called a "summer tour" of the UK, appeared on podcasts and announced a series of eye-catching policies, mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

But things are about to get a lot tougher, with MPs finally getting a chance to grill the new PM when he makes a statement to Parliament on his priorities as PM.

He has taken questions from MPs in the Commons before, when he was a minister in Tony Blair and Gordon Brown's Labour governments.

But Tuesday will be his first appearance on the government front bench for 16 years.

The team around Burnham view the start of his premiership as successful but say they will be relieved to get back to the "structure" of parliamentary politics.

Burnham will know he has really arrived as PM when he makes his debut at prime minister's questions (PMQs) on Wednesday, after almost two decades of trying to get there.

A packed Commons chamber, with curveball questions, hostile opposition politicians and the biggest TV and online audience of the week will be a world away from his nine years as Mayor of Greater Manchester.

One Number 10 source said Burnham's debut would be used as a "learning exercise" to discover "what works and what doesn't".

The new PM is said to be keen to adopt a "tonal shift" at the weekly half-hour session and will attempt to bring more humour to the occasion.

Most prime ministers enter PMQs with a thick folder of notes covering what they hope is every conceivable question they might face.

Burnham likes to speak without notes, as he did in his first speech outside Downing Street, and is thought to be considering doing the same at PMQs.

His aides sound equally relaxed about the task ahead, even though the next few weeks could define his entire premiership.

One phrase being used by Burnham's inner circle to describe his approach to Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and other opposition MPs is "problem solving, not point scoring".

Badenoch will also have to recalibrate her approach to PMQs, with senior Tory aides saying Burnham is a "different proposition" to Sir Keir Starmer.

The Tory leader was increasingly combative and sharp with Sir Keir, but a senior Tory aide says Badenoch "knows that when you get a new problem you need a new solution".

Badenoch has recently accused Burnham of being a "people pleaser" who doesn't relish taking difficult decisions, a characterisation she is likely to use again in her Commons clashes with him.

The Conservatives have identified three areas on which they believe Burnham could be vulnerable to attacks: defence spending, the potential for tax rises and the early release of prisoners.

The row around prisoner early release has created arguably Burnham's most challenging moment yet.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris is expected to make a statement in Parliament early next week, announcing how the government will ensure the killers of PC Andrew Harper are not released early.

Responsibility for fixing this political problem was handed to Norris when the prime minister publicly said he was confident that his new justice secretary could find a solution.

Officials had been stressing for weeks that this was not an easy fix, and the prime minister's critics believe this could turn out to be an early example of him choosing not to take a difficult decision, which would leave some people upset and angry.

Norris's announcement is set to include measures to both free up more prison space and create legal carve-outs to make some prisoners ineligible for early release, but those inside the Ministry of Justice are determined not to allow the details to be leaked.

Message discipline is being emphasised inside the Treasury too.

The biggest moment for the Burnham government this autumn will come on 28 October, when Chancellor John Healey unveils the Budget.

Sir Keir and his chancellor Rachel Reeves were widely seen to have been damaged politically when many of the policies in their Budgets made their way into the media.

In response, Burnham's administration has put measures in place to try to stop those leaks and it's understood the Treasury is telling officials that Budget security is like national security.

Nevertheless, speculation about the Budget is likely to dominate the coming weeks in Westminster, in particular questions about what taxes could potentially be increased.

Burnham has repeatedly said he will keep Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to increase income tax, VAT or national insurance.

But the prime minister has also said there is "room for movement" on taxes within that pledge, leading the Conservatives to believe it's a fruitful topic for political attacks.

The Treasury is focused on creating a Budget that will not spook financial markets, with a senior source insisting the core themes of Healey's plans would be "fiscal discipline" and "fiscal devolution".

Healey resigned as Sir Keir's defence secretary over what he saw as a failure to adequately fund the armed forces.

It now falls to him to find the money to fund the defence investment plan, with an extra £4.7bn needed in the Budget.

Healey is not expected to set out a path to spending 3% of GDP on defence in the Budget, and will instead wait until next spring's Spending Review.

When asked if there was nervousness about potentially annoying military chiefs, a senior Treasury source said you'd be "hard-placed to find anyone sceptical" of the idea that Healey is committed to keeping the country safe.

There has also been speculation that Burnham wants to weaken the Treasury's traditionally tight grip on policies across government.

Just before Parliament broke up for summer, the government said it was transferring "local economic growth policy" from the Treasury to Burnham's new Manchester base Number 10 North.

The Treasury is downplaying the idea that Number 10 North could become in effect a rival department.

Despite predominantly focusing on domestic issues so far, Burnham will also turn his attention to foreign policy, with a visit to Downing Street by French President Emmanuel Macron.

And, finally, he will need to make sure he keeps his own troops in Parliament happier than they were under the previous management.

Many Labour backbenchers felt that Sir Keir did not listen to them enough and Burnham is expected to be far more visible in the Commons voting lobbies and tea rooms than his predecessor.

Sources say he met most Labour MPs in the weeks before he became prime minister and believes that MPs "value that bit of face time".

But there is still a divide among the more than 400 Labour MPs about what policy areas should be prioritised at a time when the financial situation looks set to be tricky for some time.

Those around the prime minister are conscious, too, of the difficult decisions that may lie ahead.

One Number 10 source said there was an acknowledgement in Downing Street that the "public's expectation bar is high and we've got to meet it".

articles.title: Bodies wash up in neighbouring India and as far as 250 miles downstream from Nepal disaster
articles.summary: Nepal's foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, warned that bodies recovered from the disaster are at risk of decomposing quickly in the heat
articles.body:
The bodies of people swept away in this week's devastating flash floods in Nepal are washing up more than a hundred miles away in India as rescue teams race against time to search for the dead and missing while facing the challenge of fast decomposing bodies.

Eight bodies have been found in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar , two northern Indian states bordering Nepal , more than 100 miles from the flood's source.

Another body was recovered in Lumbini province – still within Nepal, but some 250 miles from Rasuwa, the district hit by a 70ft wall of ice, mud and water on Wednesday morning.

Four were recovered from a river in Uttar Pradesh's Maharajganj district. Officials there said they were severely decomposed and were being held at the mortuary of a district hospital, awaiting identification.

"We are in contact with the Nepal administration regarding the matter," said Gaurav Singh Sogarwal, the district's magistrate. He said the region had also seen high water levels but that the immediate threat of flooding had now passed.

Another three bodies have been recovered from the Gandak river in Uttar Pradesh, and one more from the same river near the Valmiki Nagar Barrage in Bihar.

Most of the bodies that are now being recovered, three days after the disaster, have already decomposed beyond recognition, the authorities said. They will be buried quickly after legal formalities are completed, because of the health risk and fears of an epidemic.

"DNA samples will be collected, and the bodies will be buried in an open space," the administration of Chitwan district in southern Nepal said in a notice.

Nepal's foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said officials were concerned by the rate bodies were decomposing in the hot and humid conditions. He said the country did not need help with search and rescue , but required foreign assistance rescuing people trapped in tunnels, restoring transport and communication links where bridges had been destroyed, and identifying bodies through DNA testing and longer-term storage.

"We have already made requests for such specialised services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how," Mr Khanal told Reuters late on Friday.

The combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet has risen to 633, authorities said on Saturday, with nearly 3,000 people still missing across the two countries, including at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.

Search and rescue operations were suspended again on Saturday because of bad weather, according to Narendra Pariyar, the top bureaucrat for Rasuwa district, one of the worst-hit areas.

"Search and rescue operations have been temporarily halted because it is raining and the weather is foggy," he told Reuters, adding that the immediate focus had shifted to arranging land transport to move rescued pilgrims to Kathmandu.

More than 5,000 army and police personnel are searching Nepal for bodies and survivors. The operation was also paused on Friday over fears that a lake straddling the Nepal- China border, formed when debris from the initial glacier collapse blocked the valley's rivers, could overflow into the Lhende Khola and Trishuli rivers.

That risk has since reduced, Chinese authorities said, with satellite imagery showing water slowly draining through the blockage. Nepal is monitoring two such lakes upstream of the flood zone, and officials have warned that flood risk will persist until both fully drain.

India has sent three flights carrying about 60 tonnes of relief material to Nepal, including blankets, medicines, food and water purification tablets, and plans to send a tunnel rescue team and a medical team.

India has also offered its disaster response force and prefabricated bridges, along with technical teams to help restore connectivity, its foreign ministry said. China has called for emergency aid to disaster-hit areas of Nepal and international rescue cooperation, without elaborating on what it is sending.

The disaster is set to cost Nepal as much as a tenth of its economy to rebuild. Finance minister Swarnim Wagle estimated the reconstruction bill at between $4 billion and $5 billion, though he said this would likely be less than the roughly $9 billion spent recovering from the 2015 earthquake, Nepal's worst recorded disaster.

The floods have already damaged hydropower stations that account for more than 12 per cent of Nepal's electricity generating capacity.

The disaster was triggered on Wednesday when part of a glacier and the mountainside beneath it collapsed on Langtang Lirung, a mountain straddling the Nepal-Tibet border, sending ice, rock and mud crashing into a river below. The mountains in this part of the Himalaya have been warming at roughly five times the global average since the 1960s, with the rate of ice loss across the wider region doubling since 2000.
